###### Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills as a
lightweight way to acquire task-specific knowledge. Recent work enables
skills to evolve from task trajectories. However, these methods often
lack systematic management of evolved skills, making it difficult for
agents to reuse and accumulate skills across domains, thus limiting
performance on subsequent tasks. To reliably accumulate, reuse, and
maintain useful skills across tasks, we present Selm (Self-Evolving
Library Management), a framework that formulates skill evolution as
library-level management. Selm jointly manages skill retrieval,
updating, and lifecycle by maintaining skill confidence and utility
signals. It introduces utility-aware retrieval to select useful skills,
a Map-Reduce framework to generate targeted updates from task-specific
experience, and lifecycle controls to retain or remove skills based on
their effectiveness. These mechanisms enable the skill library to
continuously accumulate useful experience while preserving and pruning
skills across tasks, improving agent performance on complex tasks across
diverse domains. We evaluate Selm on four agent benchmarks covering
diverse tasks and execution environments, and Selm consistently
outperforms in most settings.

| --- |
|     |

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly used to solve complex
tasks across different domains. To improve agents’ behaviors on specific
tasks, recent work introduced skills ([Anthropic, 2025b](#bib.bib9)),
which are pieces of text that can be plugged into the agent context to
provide task-specific knowledge, procedures, or experience. This gives
agents a simple way to gain specialized knowledge without additional
model training.

Recent work has explored how skills can evolve as the agent runs. Early
skills were mostly static: they were written by experts or saved from
successful experiences and then kept unchanged ([Zhao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10); [Anthropic, 2025b](#bib.bib9)). More recent methods
allow agents to update skills from their execution trajectories ([Yang
et al., 2026a](#bib.bib1); [Alzubi et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Liu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib13); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib19); [Zheng et
al., 2025](#bib.bib17); [Ni et al., 2026](#bib.bib2); [Ma et al.,
2026](#bib.bib18); [Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib20); [Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib5)). After running tasks, the agent can examine which
skill worked or failed, then edit existing skills or create new ones. In
this way, skills can change with the agent’s experience and adapt to new
tasks and environments.

![Refer to caption](2610.24630v1/fig3_intro.png)

Figure 1: Prior skill-evolution methods can overwrite useful procedures
or keep weak skills retrievable, causing task failures when experience
from different tasks conflicts. Selm instead uses utility-aware
retrieval, category-wise Map–Reduce updates, and lifecycle validation to
preserve useful skills and retire ineffective ones, enabling more
reliable task completion.

However, although these evolution methods propose many strategies to
evolve skills  ([Alzubi et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib19); [Zheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib17); [Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20); [Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib5)), few of them focus
on how to manage them. A skill revision that best fits the current round
can be harmful to later processes. For instance, a skill that is unused
or unhelpful for the present task may be overwritten or discarded; once
that change is committed, a later task can never recover the deleted
skill. Meanwhile, failed or redundant skills that have remained in the
system may still be loaded, giving the agent wrong instructions. The
core problem is that existing methods always treat skill updates as
separate, one-round edits, rather than managing skills as a dynamic,
long-term library. Thus, a skill management library is needed to decide
not only how a skill should change, but also which skills should be
retrieved, which skills should be updated, and which skills should
remain in the library.

To address these limitations, we propose Selm (Self-Evolving Library
Management), a framework that manages skills as a library and jointly
controls their retrieval, updates and lifecycle. By tracking and
leveraging skill confidence and utility, Selm enables the library to
evolve with task experience and improves the performance of the agent
across complex tasks in different domains.

Specifically, Selm introduces a skill library with explicit mechanisms
for managing skill states. To dynamically evaluate skill usefulness,
each skill is associated with a confidence score and a utility score.
Confidence reflects how strongly the skill is supported by update
operations, while utility reflects how useful it has been across tasks.
These mechanisms provide a clear basis for deciding which skills should
stay active, which skills should be removed, and which failed skills
should not be added again. The library can thus keep a skill that is
unused on the current task but still useful later, and drop one that
keeps failing, instead of committing every local edit, enabling
reliable, long-term skill management.

Second, Selm designs a Map-Reduce framework for skill updates. Applying
every trajectory to all the skills will make experience from different
types of task overwrites each other. Selm therefore groups execution
trajectories by task category(Map) and analyzes each group separately,
identifying which skills are affected and what changes are needed. It
then combines these analyses into operations(Reduce), such as adding new
skills, editing existing ones, and deleting those that no longer help.
All these operations apply only to the relevant skills and unrelated
skills are left unchanged, so a change that helps the current category
won’t erase skills required later, which enhances skill effectiveness.

Third, Selm proposes utility-aware skill retrieval. Existing methods
mainly retrieve skills based on their semantic relevance to the current
task ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib21)), which overlooks whether the
skill has been useful in previous tasks. Selm leverages historical
utility to enhance skill retrieval. It first selects skills from the
same task category and then ranks them by their relevance to the current
task and their past usefulness. This helps the agent distinguish skills
that are relevant to task on hand and have proven useful through
previous execution experience, thus enabling more effective skill
selection.

Finally, we evaluate Selm on four agent benchmarks covering diverse
execution environments and areas. Selm achieves state-of-the-art results
among skill-evolution methods, outperforming both single-document
optimization and prior multi-skill baselines without updating model
parameters.

Our contributions are (1) introducing a skill library that tracks skill
confidence and utility, managing skill validation, retention, and
removal, enabling reliable skill management throughout the evolution
process; (2) designing a Map-Reduce framework that analyzes trajectories
by task category and generates targeted operations, allowing the agent
to update relevant skills based on task-specific experience; and
(3) developing a utility-aware retrieval method that ranks skills using
both task relevance and historical utility, enabling the agent to select
skills that are both relevant and useful. Across our experiments, Selm
outperforms existing skill optimization methods, demonstrating the
effectiveness of the proposed framework.

## 2 Related Work

#### Skill construction and evolution.

Recent work has increasingly explored constructing and evolving textual
skills from agent experience, moving beyond manually specified or static
skill representations ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib10); [Anthropic,
2025b](#bib.bib9)). More broadly, approaches such as
TextGrad ([Yuksekgonul et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)) and GEPA ([Agrawal et
al., 2026](#bib.bib7)) optimize textual instructions through feedback
without updating model parameters, while Dynamic Cheatsheet ([Suzgun et
al., 2026](#bib.bib8)) and ACE ([Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib14))
iteratively refine textual context from agent experience. Building on
this paradigm, SkillOpt and SkillGrad optimize a shared skill document
or skill package by repeatedly editing textual knowledge based on
execution feedback ([Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib1); [Wang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib25)). Other approaches distill execution trajectories into
standalone lessons, strategic principles, or verified skills, thereby
converting individual experiences into reusable knowledge ([Zhao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib10); [Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib24); [Ni et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2); [Ma et al., 2026](#bib.bib18); [Qiu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib26)). Rather than maintaining a single shared artifact,
SkillWeaver ([Zheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)), EvoSkill ([Alzubi et
al., 2026](#bib.bib3)), SkillEvolver ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib19)), Memento-Skills ([Zhou et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)),
and CoEvoSkills ([Zhang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib5)) construct collections
of specialized skills to capture different task types or capabilities.
Complementary approaches construct skills from external domain resources
or learn skill-related policies through interaction and
co-training ([Yang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib21); [Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib13); [Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib22); [Jiang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib23)). Despite these advances, existing methods primarily
focus on how skills are created or improved, treating skill evolution as
a sequence of local construction or editing operations. This becomes
limiting when multiple skills coexist: updates to a shared artifact can
introduce conflicting changes, while independently accumulated skills
provide limited mechanisms for determining which skills should be
updated.

#### Skill library management.

Early work such as Voyager ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib16)) and
ExpeL ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib10)) retrieves executable or
experiential knowledge according to the relevance of the current task.
Subsequent systems make skill selection more behavior-aware and
introduce mechanisms for validating candidate skills or deciding whether
updates should be merged, accepted, or discarded ([Zhou et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20); [Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib1); [Yang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib21); [Alzubi et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib5); [Qiu et al., 2026](#bib.bib26)). More recent work
explicitly considers the maintenance of the skill library itself.
SkillOps studies how an existing skill collection can be periodically
reorganized to address issues that emerge as the library grows ([Pu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib27)), while MUSE-Autoskill organizes skill creation,
catalog retrieval, per-skill memory, and test-driven refinement into
successive lifecycle stages ([Lin et al., 2026](#bib.bib28)). Lifelong
evaluations further suggest that usage frequency alone is insufficient
to characterize the utility of a skill, motivating more explicit
utility-aware management ([Zhang et al., 2026d](#bib.bib29)). However,
these approaches generally address retrieval, validation, update
selection, or lifecycle maintenance as separate mechanisms, rather than
jointly optimizing them as coupled decisions over a continually evolving
skill library.

## 3 Preliminary

This section introduces the basic concepts of skills, skill retrieval,
and skill evolution.

#### Skill.

The $`k`$-th skill is represented as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       s_{k}=(n,d,c,t,\gamma),
       ```                      |     | (1) |

where $`n(s)`$, $`d(s)`$, $`c(s)`$, $`t(s)`$, and $`\gamma(s)`$ denote
the skill name, description, instruction content, trigger conditions,
and task category, respectively.

As the number of skills grows, they form a skill library, which is a
collection of reusable skills that the agent can draw on for different
tasks. Formally,

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       \mathcal{L}=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{|\mathcal{L}|}\}.
       ```                                             |     | (2) |

#### Skill retrieval.

The agent does not need to use the entire library for every task. Given
a task $`x`$, a retrieval mechanism selects a subset of skills from the
library to provide relevant instructions for the task. We denote the
retrieved skill set as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{S}(x)=\operatorname{Retrieve}(\mathcal{L},x),\qquad\mathcal{S}(x)\subseteq\mathcal{L}.
``` |  | (3) |

The selected skills are then provided to the agent as part of its
context before task execution.

#### Evolving skills.

With frozen target model $`M`$ and current library, the agent runs on
task $`x`$, and the resulting experience is written back so that the
same library can improve over iterations. $`r(\mathcal{L},x)`$
represents the score of library $`\mathcal{L}`$ on task $`x`$. Given
training, selection, and test splits $`D_{\mathrm{tr}}`$,
$`D_{\mathrm{sel}}`$, and $`D_{\mathrm{test}}`$, evolution proposes
libraries from $`D_{\mathrm{tr}}`$ and keeps the one that scores best on
$`D_{\mathrm{sel}}`$. Formally,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}^{*}=\arg\max_{\mathcal{L}\in\mathcal{C}(D_{\mathrm{tr}})}\frac{1}{|D_{\mathrm{sel}}|}\sum_{x\in D_{\mathrm{sel}}}r(\mathcal{L},x),\qquad r(\mathcal{L},x)\in[0,1]
``` |  | (4) |

where $`\mathcal{C}(D_{\mathrm{tr}})`$ is the set of libraries obtained
by evolving on the training split. The score $`r(\mathcal{L},x)`$ and
the operators that map trajectories to library edits are instantiated in
§[4](#S4 "4 Method ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization").

#### CRUD operations.

CRUD is an operational concept in databases for managing persistent
records. It stands for Create, Read, Update, and Delete. We migrate this
concept to skill management. In this paper, the library operations are
$`\mathrm{ADD}`$, $`\mathrm{EDIT}`$, $`\mathrm{UPVOTE}`$,
$`\mathrm{DOWNVOTE}`$, and $`\mathrm{DELETE}`$: $`\mathrm{ADD}`$ creates
a new skill, $`\mathrm{EDIT}`$ revises an existing skill,
$`\mathrm{UPVOTE}`$ and $`\mathrm{DOWNVOTE}`$ adjust its confidence, and
$`\mathrm{DELETE}`$ removes it from the active library.

## 4 Method

Selm freezes the target model $`M`$ and optimizes only the skill
library. At each iteration, the agent retrieves a small set of skills
from the current library, uses them to solve a batch of training tasks,
and converts the resulting trajectories into library updates. The
updated library is then evaluated on the selection set and retained only
when it passes the validation gate. This iterative process jointly
improves skill retrieval, skill updates, and library quality, with the
overall procedure summarized in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix A Iterative Library Evolution Algorithm ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization")
(Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Iterative Library Evolution Algorithm ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization")).

![Refer to caption](2610.24630v1/Main_Figure_1.png)

Figure 2: Overview of Selm. The frozen agent retrieves skills by
relevance and utility, executes tasks, and turns trajectories into
category-wise Map–Reduce updates. Candidate skills are validated on a
held-out set; accepted skills remain in the library, and low-utility
skills are retired to a graveyard that blocks their names from
returning.

For each skill, Selm manages it through two pieces of information:
confidence score and utility score. The confidence score $`v(s)`$
reflects how strongly a skill should be retained based on update
operations, while the utility score $`u(s)`$ records how useful the
skill has been across tasks. These two scores support different stages
of the library evolution process: confidence is updated by
UPVOTE/DOWNVOTE operations and used for lifecycle control, while utility
is used to guide skill retrieval and updated from execution outcomes.
Their corresponding update mechanisms are described in
§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Utility-Aware Skill Retrieval ‣ 4 Method ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization")
and
§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Skill Library Evolution ‣ 4 Method ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization"),
respectively.

### 4.1 Utility-Aware Skill Retrieval

Selm retrieves skills by jointly considering task category, task
relevance, and historical utility. For each task $`x_{i}`$, let
$`\gamma_{i}`$ denote its task category. Selm first constructs a
candidate set from the active skill set $`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$, retaining
skills whose categories match $`\gamma_{i}`$ or are marked as “general”.
It then ranks the candidates using a utility-aware retrieval score and
selects the top-$`k`$ skills for injection. Formally,

|     |                                                          |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       R(s,x_{i})=(1-w_{u})R_{\mathrm{rel}}(s,x_{i})+w_{u}u(s),
       ```                                                       |     | (5) |

where $`R_{\mathrm{rel}}(s,x_{i})`$ measures the relevance between skill
$`s`$ and task $`x_{i}`$ using semantic and keyword-based matching, and
$`u(s)`$ is the historical utility of the skill. The coefficient
$`w_{u}`$ controls the contribution of historical utility.

The top-$`k`$ skills are selected for task $`x_{i}`$:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{S}_{t}(x_{i})=\operatorname{top}\text{-}k\left(\left\{s\in\mathcal{S}_{t}\mid\gamma(s)\in\{\gamma_{i},\text{``general''}\}\right\},R(s,x_{i})\right).
``` |  | (6) |

The selected skills $`\mathcal{S}_{t}(x_{i})`$ are injected into the
agent context before execution. This retrieval strategy favors skills
that are both relevant to the current task and useful based on previous
execution results.

Utility Feedback. The utility score measures how useful a skill has been
on the tasks that used it. Let $`\mathcal{T}(s)`$ denote the set of
tasks whose retrieved skill set contains $`s`$. The average reward of
$`s`$ in the current update is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{r}_{s}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}(s)|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{T}(s)}r(\mathcal{L}_{t},x).
``` |  | (7) |

We update the utility using an exponential moving average (EMA)

|     |                                                 |     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       u(s)\leftarrow(1-\alpha)u(s)+\alpha\bar{r}_{s},
       ```                                              |     | (8) |

where $`\alpha`$ controls the contribution of new observations. The same
utility score is then used by the retrieval mechanism in the next
iteration. Thus, utility provides a feedback signal across successive
retrieval rounds: execution outcomes update the utility of the skills
that were used, and the resulting utility is subsequently incorporated
into retrieval, reducing the selection of ineffective skills and
improving agent performance across tasks.

### 4.2 Skill Library Evolution

After retrieving skills for each task, Selm runs the frozen target model
and uses the resulting trajectories to update the skill library. The
update process consists of four steps: rollout, trajectory analysis,
CRUD synthesis, and candidate construction.

Rollout and Reward. For each training task $`x_{i}`$, the selected
skills $`\mathcal{S}_{t}(x_{i})`$ are injected into the agent context.
Given the frozen target model $`M`$ and execution harness $`h`$, the
rollout produces a trajectory and task scores:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\left(\tau_{i},r_{\mathrm{hard},i},r_{\mathrm{soft},i}\right)=h\left(M,x_{i},\mathcal{S}_{t}(x_{i})\right),
``` |  | (9) |

where $`r_{\mathrm{hard},i}\in\{0,1\}`$ indicates whether the task
$`x_{i}`$ is fully solved, and $`r_{\mathrm{soft},i}\in[0,1]`$ measures
partial progress in two ways: When the task $`x_{i}`$ is judged by
multiple checks,
$`r_{\mathrm{soft},i}=n_{\mathrm{pass},i}/n_{\mathrm{total},i}`$, and
$`r_{\mathrm{hard},i}=1`$ only when every check passes. When a task is
judged by comparing a prediction with a reference answer,
$`r_{\mathrm{soft},i}`$ is their token-level overlap and
$`r_{\mathrm{hard},i}`$ is exact match.

The reward used for library optimization is obtained from these task
scores:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
r_{i}=r(\mathcal{L}_{t},x_{i})=\mathcal{G}\left(r_{\mathrm{hard},i},r_{\mathrm{soft},i}\right),
``` |  | (10) |

where

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{G}(r_{\mathrm{hard}},r_{\mathrm{soft}})=\begin{cases}r_{\mathrm{hard}},&\text{if metric}=\text{hard},\\
r_{\mathrm{soft}},&\text{if metric}=\text{soft},\\
(1-w)r_{\mathrm{hard}}+wr_{\mathrm{soft}},w\in[0,1],&\text{if metric}=\text{mixed}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (11) |

Each rollout therefore yields two signals for library evolution. The
trajectory $`\tau_{i}`$ is the execution evidence, including the agent’s
actions, tool calls, intermediate outputs, and errors. The scalar reward
$`r_{i}`$ shows how much of the task was solved. Later updates read
$`\tau_{i}`$ to decide what to change, and use $`r_{i}`$ to decide which
trajectories are worth changing from.

Trajectory Selection. Selm prioritizes trajectories whose observed
rewards differ substantially from the historical utility of the
retrieved skills. For task $`x_{i}`$, we compute the average utility of
its retrieved skills:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{u}(\mathcal{S}_{t}(x_{i}))=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{t}(x_{i})|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{t}(x_{i})}u(s),
``` |  | (12) |

and define the diagnostic priority as

|     |                                                           |     |      |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       p_{i}=\left|r_{i}-\bar{u}(\mathcal{S}_{t}(x_{i}))\right|.
       ```                                                        |     | (13) |

Selm selects the highest-priority trajectories for further analysis.
Trajectories with large $`p_{i}`$ provide stronger evidence that the
retrieved skills may need to be updated.
$`\bar{u}(\mathcal{S}_{t}(x_{i}))`$ is the library’s current belief
about those skills, and a large gap means the observed reward may
contradict that belief. A much higher $`r_{i}`$ shows a successful
pattern that the stored utility under-credits, and a much lower
$`r_{i}`$ shows that the retrieved guidance failed on this task. A small
gap means the rollout agrees with the existing record, so it adds little
new information about what to change.

Map—Category-wise Analysis. The selected trajectories are partitioned by
task category and analyzed independently. For each category, a
TrajectoryAnalyst identifies successful patterns, failure patterns, and
new insights from the corresponding trajectories. The analysis prevents
experience from unrelated task categories from being directly mixed
during skill updates.

Reduce—Skill update. Given the category-wise trajectory analyses and the
current skill library, a SkillSynthesizer generates a bounded set of
CRUD operations. The synthesizer considers the current skill content,
confidence, utility, and category-specific execution feedback when
deciding how to update the library.

Given a set of trajectories, Selm updates the library through the CRUD
operations introduced in
§[3](#S3 "3 Preliminary ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization"):

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{A}=\{\mathrm{ADD},\mathrm{EDIT},\mathrm{UPVOTE},\mathrm{DOWNVOTE},\mathrm{DELETE}\}.
``` |  | (14) |

For an existing skill $`s`$, the confidence score is updated as

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
v(s)\leftarrow\begin{cases}v(s)+1,&\text{for }\mathrm{UPVOTE},\\
v(s)-1,&\text{for }\mathrm{DOWNVOTE}.\end{cases}
``` |  | (15) |

The generated operations are applied to the relevant skills:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}^{\prime}_{t}=\operatorname{Apply}\left(\mathcal{L}_{t},\mathrm{ops}_{t}\right),\qquad\mathrm{ops}_{t}\subseteq\mathcal{A}.
``` |  | (16) |

When a category exhibits recurring failure patterns, the synthesizer can
also create new skills that describe strategies for avoiding these
failures. The resulting candidate library $`\mathcal{L}^{\prime}_{t}`$
is then passed to the validation stage.

Multi-timescale Updates. Following prior work on iterative skill
evolution ([Yang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib1)), Selm uses both fast and
slow updates. Fast updates are performed after each training batch to
incorporate recent trajectory feedback, while slow updates are performed
less frequently across epochs to consolidate changes that persist over
time. We also allow slow updates to produce meta skills, which summarize
persistent cross-skill patterns identified across an epoch. This allows
the library to respond to recent task feedback while reducing
unnecessary updates caused by short-term fluctuations.

### 4.3 Skill Lifecycle Management

Selm treats skill maintenance as an explicit lifecycle process, using
validation, utility tracking, and retirement mechanisms to prevent
ineffective skills from accumulating or re-entering the library.
Throughout optimization, the active set $`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$ of
$`\mathcal{L}_{t}`$ and the graveyard $`\mathbf{G}_{t}`$ obey three
structural invariants:

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle|\mathcal{S}_{t}|`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq M_{\max}`$ |  | $`\displaystyle\text{(capacity)},`$ |  | (17) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall s_{i},s_{j}\in\mathcal{S}_{t},\ i\neq j`$ | $`\displaystyle\implies n(s_{i})\neq n(s_{j})`$ |  | $`\displaystyle\text{(uniqueness)},`$ |  | (18) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\forall s\in\mathcal{S}_{t},\ n(s)`$ | $`\displaystyle\notin\{n(g)\mid g\in\mathbf{G}_{t}\}`$ |  | $`\displaystyle\text{(graveyard blocking)}.`$ |  | (19) |

Capacity bounds the store; uniqueness forbids duplicate names in
$`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$; graveyard blocking forbids reintroducing a retired
name.

Validation. A candidate update is not directly added to the active
library. Selm first evaluates the candidate library
$`\mathcal{L}^{\prime}_{t}`$ on the selection set $`D_{\mathrm{sel}}`$
using the frozen target model and the same execution harness. Its
validation score is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
V(\mathcal{L}^{\prime}_{t})=\frac{1}{|D_{\mathrm{sel}}|}\sum_{x\in D_{\mathrm{sel}}}r(\mathcal{L}^{\prime}_{t},x).
``` |  | (20) |

The candidate library is retained only when it improves the validation
performance over the current library. This validation gate prevents
updates that appear reasonable from the trajectory analysis but reduce
the actual task performance from being incorporated into the library.

Pruning and Graveyard. Selm sets a threshold $`\tau_{u}`$ for utility
score. For skill $`s`$, if $`u(s)<\tau_{u}`$ or $`v(s)<0`$, it will be
retired from the active set $`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$ and moved to the
graveyard $`\mathbf{G}_{t}`$. Retired skills are excluded from future
retrieval and cannot simply be reintroduced under the same identity.
This prevents ineffective skills from repeatedly entering and leaving
the library and keeps the active library compact.

## 5 Experiments

We evaluate Selm as a library-level optimizer for frozen agents. The
experiments answer three questions. (i) Does a managed skill library
improve over no skill, static skills, prompt evolution, single-document
skill optimization, and recent multi-skill methods? (ii) Does that
comparison hold across different models? (iii) Which library-management
controls are required for the gains?

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

Baselines. We compare against No skill; Human skill (an expert-written
document per benchmark); LLM skill (a one-shot skill from
Claude-Opus-4.6 that is never updated); prompt-evolution GEPA ([Agrawal
et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)); skill-construction methods
SkillEvolver ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib19)), Memento-Skills ([Zhou
et al., 2026](#bib.bib20)), and Trace2Skill ([Ni et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)); single-document SkillOpt ([Yang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib1)); and, under Claude Code, folder-based
EvoSkill ([Alzubi et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). EvoSkill is omitted from
the no-harness block because it assumes a SKILL.md package layout.
Qwen3-30B-A3B is evaluated only without a harness.

Benchmarks. We use four datasets: SkillsBench ([Li et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15)), SpreadsheetBench ([Ma et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)),
OfficeQA ([Opsahl-Ong et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)), and LiveMath ([He et
al., 2026](#bib.bib12)). Detailed descriptions are in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Benchmark Details ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization").

Target models. We use Claude-Opus-4.6 ([Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib31)),
DeepSeek-V4-Pro ([DeepSeek-AI, 2026](#bib.bib32)), and
Qwen3-30B-A3B ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib33)) as frozen target models.
Claude and DeepSeek are evaluated both without a harness and inside
Claude Code ([Anthropic, 2025a](#bib.bib30)); Qwen3-30B-A3B is evaluated
only without a harness. No-harness runs prepend retrieved skills to the
system prompt. Claude Code loads skills through the native agent
workspace. All methods in a given cell use the same target model,
harness, and scorer.

Hyperparameters. Hyperparameters are reported in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Hyperparameter Summary ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization").

Table 1: Main results on SkillsBench, OfficeQA, SpreadsheetBench, and
LiveMath. SkillsBench reports soft/hard accuracy (%); other rows are
accuracy (%). The best cell in each row within a model block is bold and
shaded purple; the second-best cell is shaded a lighter purple. Note:
Qwen3-30B-A3B failed all the tasks on SkillsBench, so the Hard Acc is
not included.

Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Main Results ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization")
shows that Selm consistently improves agent performance across different
benchmarks and target models. Compared with no-skill baseline and
existing skill optimization methods, Selm achieves substantial gains in
both no-harness and Claude Code settings, demonstrating the
effectiveness of managing skills as a structured library rather than
optimizing a single shared document. The improvements are also
consistent across Claude-Opus-4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Qwen3-30B-A3B,
suggesting that the benefit of library-level optimization is not tied to
a specific target model. Meanwhile, Static human-written skills and
one-shot LLM skills provide only limited improvements, while
trajectory-driven methods perform better but remain below Selm. This
indicates that the main benefit comes from continuously managing which
skills should be retrieved, updated, and retired. In particular, the
advantage is more pronounced in heterogeneous settings such as
SkillsBench, where task-specific feedback can conflict when compressed
into a single skill document.

Table 3: Skill library evolution on SpreadsheetBench (Qwen3-30B-A3B, no

Figure 3: (a) Sensitivity to the EMA decay $`\alpha`$ on
SpreadsheetBench (Claude-Opus-4.6, no harness); the marked default is
$`\alpha{=}0.4`$. (b) SkillsBench soft accuracy (%) for each target
model $`M`$ under different optimizers $`O`$, including the no-skill
baseline (no harness).

We ablate three aspects of Selm: library-management components, utility
estimation, and optimizer–target model interaction. We first remove
individual management mechanisms, including validation, utility-aware
retrieval, meta skills, slow updates, and the graveyard. We then vary
the EMA decay factor $`\alpha`$ to examine the sensitivity of utility
estimation. Finally, we vary the optimizer and target models to study
how optimizer capability affects the resulting skill library. Unless
otherwise specified, the experiments follow the default configuration.

Library-management controls are critical to the effectiveness of skill
evolution.
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization")
shows that removing the validation gate causes the largest single drop,
while removing the utility score and utility-aware retrieval reduces
only 2.9 points. Removing both meta skills and slow updates also leads
to a large degradation, compared with 53.1% when removing meta skills
alone. The graveyard provides a smaller but consistent gain, with
accuracy dropping to 50.4% without it. These results show that
validation, utility-aware selection, and longitudinal library updates
are important for preventing ineffective skill changes from
accumulating.

Selm is relatively insensitive to the EMA decay factor around the
default setting. As shown in
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization")(a),
$`\alpha{=}0.4`$ achieves 56.5% accuracy, while $`\alpha{=}0.2`$ and
$`0.6`$ obtain 55.1% and 55.3%, respectively. More extreme values,
$`\alpha{=}0.1`$ and $`0.8`$, reduce accuracy to 52.4% and 53.1%. This
indicates that the performance gain is not dependent on a narrowly tuned
smoothing coefficient.

A stronger optimizer generally produces a more effective skill library,
while weaker optimizers can still benefit stronger target models.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization")(b)
shows that, with Qwen3-30B-A3B as the target, replacing the optimizer
with DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Claude-Opus-4.6 increases soft accuracy from
20.45% to 24.75% and 31.34%, respectively. The same trend holds for
DeepSeek-V4-Pro as the target. Meanwhile, using Qwen3-30B-A3B as the
optimizer still improves Claude-Opus-4.6 from the no-skill baseline.

### 5.4 Library Evolution Analysis

Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization")
shows how the skill library changes during evolution on SpreadsheetBench
with Qwen3-30B-A3B. The initial library contains 5 skills and achieves
17.5% accuracy on the selection set. In Epoch 1, five new skills are
added, but the accuracy remains unchanged. This shows that simply adding
more skills does not improve performance. In Epoch 2, only two new
skills are added while four skills are downvoted, and the accuracy
increases to 30.0%. The slow update then makes two edits, adds two meta
skills, and downvotes two more skills. Three skills are eventually moved
to the graveyard because their confidence becomes non-positive, and they
are therefore excluded from future retrieval. The final library achieves
36.43% accuracy, compared with 30.0% for the no-skill baseline. These
changes show that the library does not improve simply by growing in
size; useful skills are added, while skills that repeatedly receive
negative feedback are removed or revised.

## 6 Conclusion

We propose Selm, a framework that manages skills as a library. Selm
tracks skill confidence and utility, validates skill updates, and
retires failed skills. Through the Map-Reduce framework and
utility-aware retrieval, Selm helps the agent select the most relevant
and effective skills. Various experiments validate that Selm
consistently improves frozen agents over prior skill-optimization
methods and achieves the strongest performance in most settings.

## Appendix A Iterative Library Evolution Algorithm

Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix A Iterative Library Evolution Algorithm ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization")
summarizes the Selm loop in
§[4](#S4 "4 Method ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization"):
utility-aware retrieval and rollout, diagnostic trajectory selection,
Map–Reduce CRUD synthesis, validation gating, pruning to the graveyard,
and slow updates.

0:  Frozen target model $`M`$, execution harness $`h`$, training split
$`D_{\mathrm{tr}}`$, selection split $`D_{\mathrm{sel}}`$, epochs $`E`$,
retrieval budget $`K`$, trajectory budget $`B`$, EMA coefficient
$`\alpha`$, utility weight $`w_{u}`$, retirement threshold $`\tau_{u}`$,
maximum capacity $`M_{\max}`$

1:  $`L_{0}\leftarrow`$ initial skill library $`\triangleright`$ empty
or seed skills

2:  $`G_{0}\leftarrow\emptyset`$ $`\triangleright`$ graveyard starts
empty

3:  $`L_{\mathrm{best}}\leftarrow L_{0}`$ $`\triangleright`$ snapshot
kept for export

4:  $`V_{\mathrm{best}}\leftarrow V(L_{0})`$ $`\triangleright`$ score on
$`D_{\mathrm{sel}}`$

5:  for $`e=1,\ldots,E`$ do

6:   for each training batch $`\mathcal{B}\subset D_{\mathrm{tr}}`$
$`\triangleright`$ one fast update do

7:
   $`S_{t}\leftarrow\{s\in L_{t}:n(s)\notin\{n(g)\mid g\in G_{t}\}\}`$
$`\triangleright`$ block retired names

8:    for each task $`x_{i}\in\mathcal{B}`$ do

9:     Let $`\gamma_{i}`$ be the category of $`x_{i}`$

10:
    $`S_{t}(x_{i})\leftarrow\operatorname{TopK}\bigl(\{s\in S_{t}:\gamma(s)\in\{\gamma_{i},\mathrm{general}\}\},R(s,x_{i}),K\bigr)`$
$`\triangleright`$ utility-aware retrieval

11:
    $`(\tau_{i},r_{\mathrm{hard},i},r_{\mathrm{soft},i})\leftarrow h(M,x_{i},S_{t}(x_{i}))`$
$`\triangleright`$ rollout

12:
    $`r_{i}\leftarrow\mathcal{G}(r_{\mathrm{hard},i},r_{\mathrm{soft},i})`$
$`\triangleright`$ scalar reward

13:     $`p_{i}\leftarrow\bigl|r_{i}-\bar{u}(S_{t}(x_{i}))\bigr|`$
$`\triangleright`$ gap from stored utility

14:    end for

15:    Select the top-$`B`$ trajectories according to $`p_{i}`$
$`\triangleright`$ most informative traces

16:    for each skill $`s`$ used in the current batch do

17:     $`u(s)\leftarrow(1-\alpha)u(s)+\alpha\bar{r}_{s}`$
$`\triangleright`$ EMA utility

18:    end for

19:    Partition selected trajectories by task category
$`\triangleright`$ Map

20:    for each category $`c`$ do

21:
    $`a_{c}\leftarrow\operatorname{TrajectoryAnalyst}(\text{trajectories of }c,L_{t})`$
$`\triangleright`$ success, failure, insights

22:    end for

23:
   $`\mathrm{ops}_{t}\leftarrow\operatorname{SkillSynthesizer}(\{a_{c}\},L_{t})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Reduce; operation budgets

24:
   $`L^{\prime}_{t}\leftarrow\operatorname{Apply}(L_{t},\mathrm{ops}_{t},G_{t})`$
$`\triangleright`$ candidate library

25:    Evaluate
$`V(L^{\prime}_{t})=\frac{1}{|D_{\mathrm{sel}}|}\sum_{x\in D_{\mathrm{sel}}}r(L^{\prime}_{t},x)`$
$`\triangleright`$ validation gate

26:    if $`V(L^{\prime}_{t})>V(L_{t})`$ then

27:     $`L_{t}\leftarrow L^{\prime}_{t}`$ $`\triangleright`$ accept
only if improved

28:    end if

29:    if $`V(L_{t})>V_{\mathrm{best}}`$ then

30:     $`L_{\mathrm{best}}\leftarrow L_{t}`$ $`\triangleright`$ keep
the best snapshot

31:     $`V_{\mathrm{best}}\leftarrow V(L_{t})`$

32:    end if

33:   end for

34:   if slow update is scheduled at epoch $`e`$ $`\triangleright`$ less
frequent than fast updates then

35:    Generate additional CRUD operations $`\triangleright`$
consolidate persistent trends

36:
   $`L^{\prime}_{t}\leftarrow\operatorname{Apply}(L_{t},\mathrm{ops}^{\mathrm{slow}}_{t},G_{t})`$

37:    Validate $`L^{\prime}_{t}`$ on $`D_{\mathrm{sel}}`$
$`\triangleright`$ same gate as the fast update

38:    if $`V(L^{\prime}_{t})>V(L_{t})`$ then

39:     $`L_{t}\leftarrow L^{\prime}_{t}`$

40:    end if

41:    if $`V(L_{t})>V_{\mathrm{best}}`$ then

42:     $`L_{\mathrm{best}}\leftarrow L_{t}`$

43:     $`V_{\mathrm{best}}\leftarrow V(L_{t})`$

44:    end if

45:   end if

46:   Lifecycle pruning:

47:   for each $`s\in L_{t}`$ do

48:    if $`u(s)<\tau_{u}`$ or $`v(s)\leq 0`$ $`\triangleright`$ low
utility or non-positive confidence then

49:     $`L_{t}\leftarrow L_{t}\setminus\{s\}`$

50:     $`G_{t}\leftarrow G_{t}\cup\{s\}`$ $`\triangleright`$ retire;
name cannot return

51:    end if

52:   end for

53:   Enforce $`|G_{t}|\leq|G|_{\max}`$ $`\triangleright`$ graveyard
capacity

54:   Enforce $`|S_{t}|\leq M_{\max}`$, name uniqueness, and graveyard
blocking

55:  end for

56:  return $`L_{\mathrm{best}}`$ $`\triangleright`$ not necessarily the
last $`L_{t}`$

Algorithm 1 Selm — Iterative Library Evolution

## Appendix B Benchmark Details

We evaluate on four agent benchmarks covering heterogeneous domains,
procedural tool use, long-context document reasoning, and mathematical
problem solving.

SkillsBench ([Li et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)): a multi-domain benchmark
with 8 task categories (cybersecurity, data analysis, finance-economics,
hardware engineering, natural science, social science, software
engineering, and one general category). SkillsBench reports both hard
accuracy and soft accuracy, corresponding to $`r_{\mathrm{hard}}`$ and
$`r_{\mathrm{soft}}`$ in
§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Utility-Aware Skill Retrieval ‣ 4 Method ‣ Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization").

SpreadsheetBench ([Ma et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)): spreadsheet
manipulation requiring multi-step formula generation and cell-level
operations.

OfficeQA ([Opsahl-Ong et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)): a grounded reasoning
benchmark built from U.S. Treasury Bulletins with a corpus of
approximately 89,000 pages.

LiveMath ([He et al., 2026](#bib.bib12)):
LiveMathematicianBench(LiveMath), a live mathematician-level reasoning
benchmark, abbreviated LiveMath in tables.

The last three benchmarks report a single accuracy.

## Appendix C Hyperparameter Summary

|                         |                                           |         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------|---------|
| Hyperparameter          | Description                               | Default |
| $`M_{\max}`$            | Maximum library capacity                  | 30      |
| $`w_{u}`$               | Utility weight in retrieval scoring       | 0.6     |
| $`w`$                   | soft score weight in reward calculating   | 0.5     |
| $`\alpha`$              | EMA decay factor for utility update       | 0.4     |
| $`\tau_{\text{soft}}`$  | Soft threshold for success classification | 0.3     |
| $`|\mathbf{G}|_{\max}`$ | Maximum graveyard capacity                | 50      |
| $`B_{\text{ADD}}`$      | Max ADD operations per evolution step     | 5       |
| $`B_{\text{EDIT}}`$     | Max EDIT operations per evolution step    | 3       |
| $`K`$                   | Number of skills retrieved per task       | 3       |
| $`B`$                   | Trajectory selection budget               | 50      |
| $`N_{slow}`$            | Slow update sample size                   | 20      |
| $`\tau_{u}`$            | threshold for utility score               | 0.05    |
| Injection budget        | Max characters for skill injection        | 2000    |
| Fail compression        | Max chars for failed trajectories         | 2000    |
| Success compression     | Max chars for successful trajectories     | 400     |
| Map parallelism         | Max parallel TrajectoryAnalyst workers    | 16      |

## Appendix E Limitations and Future Work

Semantic deduplication. The graveyard mechanism operates at the name
level (exact string match), preventing exact-name oscillation but not
semantically equivalent skills with different names from coexisting.
Embedding-based similarity detection would be a natural extension.

Cross-environment transfer. A skill library optimized on one benchmark
could potentially warm-start optimization on another, analogous to
transfer learning in neural networks. We leave exploration of
cross-benchmark transfer to future work.

Scalability. While we demonstrate effectiveness with up to 30 skills
across 8 categories, scaling to hundreds of categories or thousands of
skills would require more sophisticated indexing (e.g., embedding-based
retrieval) and potentially hierarchical library organization.

Optimizer model dependence. The quality of evolution depends on the
optimizer LLM’s ability to analyze trajectories and synthesize CRUD
operations. Weaker optimizer models may produce lower-quality
operations, and the interaction between optimizer capability and library
quality deserves systematic study.
````
